claims.text: Pack-cementation aluminizing will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of a refractory high-entropy alloy relative to the untreated alloy.
An aluminum-rich pack-cementation treatment introduces aluminum into the alloy surface by diffusion.
The introduced aluminum promotes formation of a dense, adherent alumina layer during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
The relevant service condition is approximately 1000°C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere for several hundred hours.
Aluminizing produces a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
Aluminum at the treated surface reacts with oxygen to form a protective alumina layer.
The alumina layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion through the alumina layer substantially reduces further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
Under identical exposure conditions, the aluminized alloy will show lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated alloy.
Under identical exposure conditions, the aluminized alloy will form a more stable and adherent oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy develops a less protective and potentially more porous oxide scale during high-temperature oxygen exposure.
The less protective oxide scale on the untreated alloy leads to greater oxidation weight gain.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on alloy composition and pack-cementation processing parameters.
Long-term alumina-scale adhesion under cyclic thermal conditions has not been established.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing aluminized and untreated specimens at approximately 1000°C for 500 hours in an oxygen-containing atmosphere.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence, non-uniformity, or poor adhesion of the alumina scale relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
